articles.title: Trump’s Politicized Deportations Are Becoming the Global Norm
articles.author: Branko Marcetic
articles.content: Given all the headlines about the US government trying to deport one or another migrant over their foreign policy views, you’d be forgiven for thinking this is a uniquely Trumpian innovation. Sadly, as the recent developments out of Latvia show, it’s far from it. Yesterday news broke that Leonid Ragozin, an exiled Russian journalist who has lived in the Baltic country for over a decade (and is also a Jacobin contributor who I interviewed for a forthcoming piece) has been declared persona non grata by the Latvian government, which intends to swiftly deport him. The Latvian foreign minister cited unspecified “information” received from “the competent authorities” to justify this extraordinary measure, but you barely have to even read between the lines to see that Ragozin’s offense was simply having opinions and doing reporting that the Latvian elite don’t like. For one, there’s the fact that Latvia’s own interior minister, Jānis Dombrava, came right out and said this, complaining last week that Ragozin had “over a prolonged period of time, publicly expressed opinions that are in blatant contradiction to the interests of the Latvian state.” You’ll note that this rationale is eerily similar to the words that Donald Trump’s State Department has used to claim the power to strip permanent residency from and deport pro-Palestinian activists Mahmoud Khalil and Mohsen Mahdawi: that they hold views that might have “serious adverse foreign policy consequences” for the United States. That Ragozin is being targeted for his journalism and opinions is made even less in doubt by the fact that several news reports based on information fed by European officials all mention a recent interview Ragozin did with Aaron Maté for the podcast Useful Idiots , clips of which have then been circulated online and cited by anti-Russia accounts that exist to harass anyone not toeing a sufficiently pro-war line on Ukraine. Ragozin’s critics have charged variously that he’s an “ apologist of Moscow’s war against Ukraine,” that he “push[es] aggressively pro-Russian lies ,” or, in the words of the Latvian politician who suggested he be deported in the first place, says things that reflect Russian propaganda about the war in Ukraine and so was actually playing a role in Russian “hybrid warfare” activities. (Yes, a politician really said this). You may not be shocked to find out that this is all complete and utter nonsense. Ragozin has done a lot of writing, so it is not remotely difficult to quickly bring up a long paper trail of all the times he has criticized Vladimir Putin and his horrendous war. The day Russia invaded Ukraine, Ragozin called it “a crime against Ukraine” and a “brazen violation of international law” that “will mark a dark chapter in Russia’s history.” He also called it “insanely criminal” and “ all-out aggression ” and accused Putin, who he has called “horrible,” of having “unleashed evil.” In a piece for The Washington Post early in the war, he dismantled he war propaganda fed by the Kremlin to the Russian public, telling readers that “Russians are not facing an existential threat now, of course” but rather “it is their own country that’s posing an existential threat to a neighbor.” In other posts, he’s charged “the vote was blatantly unfree” in Russian elections, mocked the nonsense math involved in Putin’s rigged elections, pointed out the gulf between the Russian leader’s sanctimonious appeal to “traditional values” and his own private behavior, and frequently lauded and defended the liberal Russian opposition leader Alexei Navalny, who was tortured and likely killed by the Putin regime. You could go on and on with this, but you get the idea. Look at what Ragozin actually said in the interview, and it’s obvious his critics are doing what the war lobby always does , including throughout the nearly five years the Ukraine war has raged: twisting his words to make his analysis seem like partisan cheerleading. Far from justifying Moscow’s actions — or lobbing a threat against Latvia, as some have claimed particularly dishonestly — Ragozin was doing what analysts and journalists do and explaining the mindset that is driving the current Russian “hybrid warfare” campaign in Europe. No, if you want to understand what Ragozin has done wrong, Latvia’s interior minister helpfully laid it out : Ragozin has, among other things, “blamed the West” for the war, “criticized the West and Ukraine,” “discredited” Ukraine’s politicians and armed forces, called the anti-Russian sanctions ineffective, and questioned if simple imperialism was really the only motivating factor behind Putin’s invasion, as Western politicians tend to insist. In other words, he has done reporting, voiced opinions, and highlighted information that are politically inconvenient for a hawkish Latvian elite — no different from how those who said September 11 was blowback for US foreign policy have been labeled pro-terrorist, or how those pointing out that the seeds for October 7 were sown in previous decades of Israeli brutalization of Gaza were labeled antisemitic pogromists. Or, as an editor at the Berlin-based Zentrum Liberale Moderne — a think tank that styles itself as “stand[ing] for the defense and renewal of liberal democracy” — helpfully summed it up : “Since 2022 he gradually transformed into a rancorous peacenik.” Weaponizing Immigration On the one hand, this is all the culmination and natural outgrowth of a toxic political discourse that’s developed around the Ukraine war and Russia. Ragozin, like all critics of this war, has for years been on the receiving end of these kinds of spurious and ugly smears, meant to cast basic foreign policy analysis as treasonous and even criminal, a trend hardly limited to the Baltics but sadly one we’ve seen across Europe and the Western world. The difference is, until this current Latvian government, no government was thuggish and shameless enough to treat these kinds of internet smears as the legal basis for something as serious as deporting someone. But there’s something else going on here. As Ragozin himself wrote yesterday, Latvian authorities are resorting to declaring him persona non grata out of “the desire to deny me justice in the court system where the case — as senior politicians involved in attacking openly admit — won’t hold water.” In other words, weaponizing the immigration system against a dissident and war critic means a much easier threshold to punish someone for doing journalism. This, too, is part of an alarming and accelerating trend, a different one. More and more, particularly in countries that are meant to be liberal democracies, we are seeing immigration policies leveraged not for their actual purpose — for managing the millennia-old, natural movement of human beings across borders in a secure and orderly fashion — but as an extralegal way to punish and censor speech. The Trump administration’s use and abuse of this move is probably most famous, targeting activists and journalists as the verbal threat of denaturalization and deportation for political views becomes a shockingly regular part of right-wing political rhetoric. But we’re seeing it pop up elsewhere. Recently, the journalists behind NAZA , the recent documentary featuring Israeli soldiers recounting the war crimes they carried out in Gaza for the past three years, were threatened by both the Israeli prime minister and culture minister with being stripped of their citizenship over their work, despite the fact that both filmmakers were born in Israel. Before that, Israeli authorities denied entry to and deported a French journalist explicitly because her work criticized Israel’s war in Gaza and used the word “apartheid” to describe its treatment of Palestinians. This past June, the French government placed under house arrest and deported Xenia Fedorova, the former head of Russian state television network RT France, who had become a critic of the Ukraine war for a conservative billionaire’s media empire, on the basis that she was a potential risk to “ national security ” and that she was acting as a “conduit for disinformation campaigns orchestrated by the Russian authorities,” even as media outlets readily admitted there was no evidence she was paid by or had any links to the Kremlin. Unlike Ragozin, Fedorova really did hew close to Moscow’s talking points — calling the war a “special military operation” for instance, the Kremlin’s preferred term for its invasion. But the rhetoric and reporting on Fedorova folded this kind of thing into legitimate points she’s raised about how NATO expansion helped spark the conflict and the Western role in prolonging the war, as if they’re all one and the same — points that are far from unique to her and have been made by many voices not friendly to the Kremlin. Her deportation opens the door to the French government deeming anyone making those inconvenient criticisms a national security threat subject to expulsion. In the UK, British conservatives demanded that recently released British-Egyptian democracy activist Alaa Abd El Fattah be stripped of his British citizenship for decade-old intemperate tweets praising the murder of Zionists — even as Israeli officials who have called for and actually carried out much worse violence are welcomed to the country. Last year, a German climate activist who already served a stiff prison sentence over a peaceful protest was facing the “ double punishment ” of being deported for it, too, and being separated from his British partner and stepfamily in the process, a case he ultimately successfully appealed . Whatever you think of each of these cases or the politics of the people involved, they reflect a rapid degradation in the Western world when it comes to the right to speak freely that’s meant to be core to liberal democracy. And they suggest Ragozin’s case, rather than being unique, is a preview of something that will become increasingly common. The Bell Will Toll for Thee Anyone cheering this should, first of all, be embarrassed. But they should also not be so naive to think that, in systems where power regularly changes hands and swings constantly between Left and Right, the targets of a policy of vindictive, politically motivated expulsion are going to stay limited to the viewpoints they personally disagree with. As I’ve written before , stripping citizenship from or expelling government critics and other dissidents used to be the behavior of the authoritarian states that Western politicians hold up as examples of what we must stop our societies from becoming, including Nazi Germany and, ironically, Putin’s Russia . But because the immigration system typically lacks the due process, evidentiary standards, and checks and balances of the criminal justice system, those same Western politicians are now increasingly turning to it as a way to punish critics while sidestepping legal protections or even having to mount a case that stands the test of a proper criminal trial. It is also one of the sad and predictable ironies of war fever, warned about at the start of the Ukraine invasion, as Western governments embarked on a program of Putin-like censorship to fight the so-called “information war” over the actual war. On that topic, maybe it’s best to give Ragozin himself the last word. “Putin’s greatest — and perhaps unintended — success in this conflict has been a profound Putinization of the Western discourse when it comes to Ukraine and Russia,” he wrote earlier this year, complaining about how it had been taken over by black and white thinking, loss of nuance, and an atmosphere where people in democracies denounced each other like they were living in occupied East Germany. “I can’t see how one can defeat the rising authoritarianism embodied by Putin with the help of Kremlin-styled intimidation, threats, online mob attacks and vile propaganda,” he concluded. “I don’t want to live in a world that’s made of different versions of Putin.” This article originally appeared in Jacobin , a democratic socialist magazine publishing long-form essays and analysis on politics, economics, and culture. articles.title: Locals 228 and 728 Defy Odds to Win Substantial Wage Increases
articles.content: On September 28 and 29 respectively, UE Locals 728 and 228 ratified new one-year agreements. The locals collectively represent over 800 workers who process visa petitions and provide petitioner support at the U.S. Department of State’s (DOS) Kentucky Consular Center (KCC) in Williamsburg, KY (Local 728), and National Visa Center (NVC) in Portsmouth, NH (Local 228). They are sister locations whose members are both employed by federal contractor LDRM under DOS’s Visa Support Services contract. The Trump Administration’s drastically increased visa application fees, regional travel bans, and newly-imposed visa bonds have driven workloads at both facilities to historic lows. Taking that into consideration, along with an impending surge in the cost of health insurance premiums, the bargaining committees of both locals made the decision to pursue one-year extensions of their current contracts and bargain exclusively over wages and fringe benefits. Despite the odds, Locals 228 and 728 won new union contracts with substantial, combined flat hourly increases of $2.10 and $1.60, which represent average gains of seven and six percent, respectively. Local 728 negotiations kicked off in Williamsburg on September 15 but got a burst of energy the following day when members onsite at KCC held a rally just minutes before the committee presented a counter-proposal. By the time the employer delivered their last, best, and final offer, several members had shown up to observe negotiations firsthand. Recalling the experience, Local 728 First Shift Chief Steward Daulton Couch noted, “Through member support and attendance backing the bargaining committee while at the table, we collectively fought and won a substantial wage increase to help combat the increased costs of everyday living as well as assist with the harsh reality that is the healthcare system in America.” Local 228 began their round of negotiations in Portsmouth, NH on September 22 by reminding the employer just how astronomically high the cost of living on the New England Seacoast had become. Determined to steer the course of negotiations the following day, members onsite at NVC took action. “When management submitted their first two passes, their proposals were identical to the first two passes they presented to our sister Local 728 a week prior,” said Local 228 Sergeant-at-Arms Dave Kirby. “When the committee called them out on their ‘mirrored bargaining’ as not bargaining at all, the membership took action. They held a walkout at their breaks on both shifts. After that, the real negotiation began. Direct action is one of the only tried and true methods to get management’s attention,” The employer delivered their last, best, and final offer to the Local 228 committee on September 23 in a packed, standing-room-only conference hall. Looking back on the locals’ joint contract campaign, Local 728 Second Shift Chief Steward Kala Collett said, "No matter how bleak the circumstances may seem, you can never forget how powerful [our] locals become when the members work together as one…and [we] have proven that during every contract bargaining." The Local 228 Bargaining Committee consisted of President Jane Shepard-O’Connor , First Shift Chief Steward Shane Tassinari , Second Shift Chief Steward Ed Martin , Sergeant-at-Arms Dave Kirby, and Stewards Dee Towne , Courtney Smith , and Danny McNair . The Local 728 Bargaining Committee consisted of President Caroline Gambrel , First Shift Chief Steward Daulton Couch, Second Shift Chief Steward Kala Collett, and stewards Brian Bradley and Ashley Perkins . They were assisted by UE Field Organizer Kevin White .

articles.title: Local 115 Wins Wage Increases, Firm Limits on Mandatory Overtime in Second UE Pact
articles.content: The members of UE Local 115 ratified a new three-year agreement on August 27 after four months of negotiations. Refresco employees bottle beverage products like Gatorade, Bodyarmor, Tropicana, and generic sodas for various supermarket chains. The contract, Local 115’s second with Refresco, includes an average 14 percent wage increase across the life of the agreement, establishes firm limits on mandatory overtime, and lowers penalties for attendance infractions. Members making less than $24.00 an hour are set to receive general wage increases of 5.5, 4.25, and 4 percent in each year respectively, with all other workers receiving 4, 3.25, and 3 percent increases. The local also won longevity pay increases, an increase to the third shift differentials, and adjustments to lead pay. Some workers are receiving as much as a 12 percent increase in the first year of the contract, 6.7 percent in the second year, and 6.3 percent in the third year. Local 115 won a limit of three mandatory same-day overtime shifts in a week, a large problem during the life of the first contract. Employees were sometimes being mandated up to five or six days during the high season. The agreement establishes reporting pay and schedule posting procedures. The local also won the right to advance notice of and the right to bargain over permanent schedule changes. This contract saw a major win on attendance procedures, an issue which was very important for the membership. Attendance infractions for arriving late or leaving early from the overtime portion of the employee’s shift will be halved going forward. An employee will now have to be tardy or leave early during the overtime position twenty-four times in a year before receiving a step one write up. Employees will also be given a ninety-minute grace period to get to work if there are government-imposed travel restrictions, and will be given seven business days to bring in medical documentation before being written up for attendance policy violations. Overall, almost half of the contract is being changed, with two brand new articles regarding ADA accommodations and immigration leave & rights ( read the full summary here ). The company entered negotiations saying they did not want to “rewrite” the contract. The local organized t-shirt days and produced union stickers saying “No te metas con nosotros. Unidos para un segundo contrato” (“Don’t tread on me. United for a second contract”). The local began collecting strike pledges when they received the Company’s first economic offer. By the last day of bargaining, over 75 percent of the plant had signed the pledges. Local 115 members also met with representatives of the New York City and New York State pension funds to discuss various issues during bargaining. Most importantly, the contract has no concessions. The union beat back attempts by the company to increase the notification period for vacation requests and the removal of holiday pay counting towards overtime calculations. Local 115 was represented in negotiations by President Ivan Rios , Plant Chief Steward Jose Rivera , John Mata , and Alexander Prendas . They were assisted by UE Field Organizer Eric Cortes-Kopp . Eastern Region President Janet Gray , General Executive Board Member Dean Pacileo from Local 243, and Local 506 President Ryan Mudger and Business Agent John Miles provided valuable advice. The Private Equity Shareholder Project coordinated various meetings with representatives of the NYS and NYC pension funds.

articles.title: UE Members Win Collective Bargaining Ordinance Despite Virginia Governor’s Veto
articles.content: On September 22, the Portsmouth City Council passed a collective bargaining ordinance allowing city workers “the right to organize, form, join, assist, and pay dues or contributions to employee organizations, to bargain collectively through an exclusive bargaining representative of their own choosing, and to engage in other concerted activities for the purpose of collective bargaining or other mutual aid and protection.” The language in the ordinance covers all city employees and prohibits retaliation for organizing. “The City will refrain from any intimidation, coercion, or harassment of employees in the exercise of their rights under this division.” The ordinance also allows workers to use work property for union activities off duty or during breaks and allows for the use of city communications and email to conduct union business. UE members and other unions in the state have been organizing around collective bargaining rights for years. The success in Portsmouth, according to UE member and Mental Health Case Manager Hope Cuffee , came from consistency. She said, “Persistence, patience, and not giving up has been so important.” Cuffee said the city firefighters who are affiliated with IAFF have been key partners in the fight. “I think that we got here because of the firefighters and us. We were constantly writing letters to city council, attending meetings, and communicating with them to let them know we wanted to be heard.” Workers from Portsmouth also attended “organizing blitzes” in North Carolina — learning alongside other union members in the South. The win in Portsmouth came only four months after Virginia Governor Abigail Spanberger vetoed a state collective bargaining bill that she initially promised to pass. In a newsletter from the Virginia UE members, Tangela Randall , an Independent Living Coordinator with Portsmouth Social Services, responded to the governor’s betrayal by saying, “The truth is that public-sector workers in Virginia have been deeply underpaid and under-appreciated for generations. This was a critical opportunity to correct a historic, racist law that was established in the Jim Crow era to hold down Black workers. It now holds back all workers.” The same newsletter said, “During her bid to win the election last fall, she looked many unionists in the eyes and committed her support for public-sector collective bargaining.” The betrayal by the governor is a reminder that UE’s policy of independent political action is the only way to advance the rights of working people. When asked about the recent actions that led up to the ordinance being passed, Randall said, “The consistency of the city workers showing up has been most important. Me and some other workers have been at city council meetings constantly to just let our presence be known. Some of the things we did were not approved but we still continued to gather.” When asked about the recent win in Portsmouth, Randall said, “We have a renewed sense of hope.” She also said that she and the other members of UE will continue to “get things rolling because one thing we do know is that election season is here… Now is not the time to slack off. It’s time to put our best foot forward, keep up the pressure, and continue to organize.” Cuffee added, “I would like to thank everyone involved. It started with a few of us and even though we started off small, our persistence made it happen. We still got more fights to go to be official but I want to thank everyone for not giving up. Even though I might retire in four years, it wasn’t about me, it was about people behind me. It was about the whole city.”

articles.title: Local 221 Ratifies Contract Amidst Federal Cuts
articles.content: At the end of September, UE Local 221 members who work for the Head Start program at Northeast Kingdom Community Action (NEKCA) ratified a two-year contract that includes wage increases and improvements to language. The benefits in the contract were won despite $1.2 million of federal funding cut to the Head Start program. The members won a $250 one-time stipend for full-time employees and a $100 stipend for part-time employees. The contract includes a 1.5 percent wage increase and the option for members to negotiate future cost-of-living adjustments during the life of the contract. The members also won layoff protections — extending the layoff recall list from 12 to 18 months for employees with one to three years of service. The bargaining team consisted of Kelli Arkley , Deborah Brousseau , Nancy McBey , and Julia Tucker . They were assisted by International Representative Sherry Bryant . articles.title: Local 119 Signs One-Year Contract
articles.content: UE Local 119, which represents approximately 200 one-on-one aides, teacher assistants, bus aides, and before and after school program attendants in the Winslow Township schools, concluded negotiations with their employer, the contractor ESS, at the end of September. The one-year contract will provide most workers with a 2.25 percent wage increase, with some senior workers receiving a three percent increase. Workers also gained a second day of bereavement leave. During contract negotiations, Local 119 members signed a petition to management demanding “to be treated with respect, earn a living wage, have decent benefits, and receive responses to our concerns.” Several members wrote individual emails to ESS management, and workers wore union buttons at a training. The Local 119 negotiating committee consisted of President Bobbie Johnson , Treasurer Ken Smith , steward Joette Duckette , Anna Gonzalez , Linda Hampton , and Crystal Robinson .
