articles.title: Under Trump Pressure, Bolivia Arrests Its Own Attorney General
articles.author: Joseph Bouchard
articles.content: Early last week, the Trump administration’s State Department announced visa restrictions on a group of Latin American officials it accused of corruption and of “undermining democratically-selected governments.” Of the twenty-one people it targeted in Bolivia, Washington chose to name only one: Bolivia’s sitting attorney general, Roger Mariaca. A little over twenty-four hours later, on September 30, Bolivian police detained Mariaca at Viru Viru International Airport in Santa Cruz while agents raided prosecutors’ offices in Sucre and Santa Cruz. He was taken without a warrant before the legislature had taken any steps to remove him from office, as required by the constitution and, as the government itself later acknowledged , with intelligence supplied by the US Drug Enforcement Administration (DEA), an agency with a particularly sordid history in Bolivia. It looked like an order sent straight from Washington. “The arrest of Bolivia’s attorney general just after the US rescinded his visa,” journalist Benjamin Swift, based in La Paz, told Jacobin , “is a clear signal of the United States’ growing influence in Bolivia.” At the time of his arrest, Mariaca was investigating the far-right Argentine political operative Fernando Cerimedo, “ MAGA’s man in Latin America,” who was arrested just over a month prior at the same airport while attempting to flee to Buenos Aires. Cerimedo was taken in for allegedly ordering a hit against his pregnant partner, the lawyer Nadia Beller, who survived the attack by two gunmen outside a Santa Cruz hotel. Mariaca’s office soon also began digging into Cerimedo’s alleged ties to drug-trafficking networks. Cerimedo, who has close connections to Donald Trump’s innermost circle, has reportedly had a hand in virtually every recent far-right electoral victory in the region, including that of Javier Milei in Argentina, José Antonio Kast in Chile, Nasry Asfura in Honduras, and Abelardo de la Espriella in Colombia. He was also deeply involved in the disinformation campaign that claimed the 2022 Brazilian election was stolen from Jair Bolsonaro, crafting a narrative that — as Sunday’s first-round election results show — continues to sway voters. In Bolivia, he was not only a strategist in right-wing President Rodrigo Paz’s campaign but became one of his top aides once in government, holding his own office in Bolivia’s presidential palace. After Cerimedo’s allies arrested Attorney General Mariaca, US Secretary of State Marco Rubio signaled the White House’s involvement and support, declaring that the Trump administration “stands firmly” with President Paz as his government takes “bold and decisive actions to combat narco-trafficking, systemic corruption, and transnational organized crime.” Attacking the Judiciary Mariaca was arrested along with thirteen others from the Public Prosecutor’s Office and the justice system, including Santa Cruz departmental prosecutor Alberto Zeballos and prosecutor Martín Irusta, in a direct attack on Bolivia’s judiciary. Former socialist President Evo Morales called the operation unconstitutional and accused the DEA, banned from the country until recently for its meddling in politics and involvement in cocaine trafficking in Bolivia, of running it. President Paz’s minister of government, Marco Antonio Oviedo, who oversees the police, pointed to Mariaca as the leader of “a criminal organization embedded in the justice system and in the administration of a very important institution in our country, the Public Ministry.” “Either you stand with the law,” Oviedo said, “or you stand with crime, with narcoterrorism” — a term borrowed directly from the Trump administration. The day before his arrest, Mariaca publicly attributed the initial US sanctions against him to his office’s investigations into Cerimedo and the gasolina basura (junk gasoline) case over contaminated fuel imports. There have been massive fuel shortages in the country since the president slashed fuel subsidies, hitting the poor the hardest. “We know the work we have been doing has not been to the liking of certain political sectors, both outside and inside our country,” Mariaca said. “The timing of Mariaca’s arrest is alarming,” Thomas Becker told Jacobin . Becker is an international human rights lawyer who led the landmark US civil case that found former Bolivian President Gonzalo Sánchez de Lozada (1993–97, 2002–3), a close Washington ally, liable for extrajudicial killings. “The US is meddling in Bolivia’s internal affairs in plain sight,” he said. “Washington is no longer even pretending to hide its hand. This is the ‘Donroe Doctrine’ in action.” Legal Maneuverings Two days after the arrest of Mariaca, both chambers of the Plurinational Legislative Assembly passed Law 1773 . It amends Article 25 of the Organic Law of the Public Ministry to let lawmakers, by a two-thirds vote, permanently suspend an attorney general who has been formally charged or placed under precautionary measures for serious crimes and name an interim replacement. Paz signed it on Friday. In a session that ran more than twenty hours , into early Saturday, 113 of the 128 legislators present voted to remove Mariaca for good, and the Assembly installed José Armando Urioste Viera as interim attorney general for ninety days. It was, in effect, a post hoc legalization of an unconstitutional removal. Vice President Edmand Lara, a populist figure who has broken with President Paz, argued that “the law is not retroactive” and that suspending officials on the strength of charges alone violates the constitutional presumption of innocence. He has so far refused to swear in Urioste. A US official attended the session as part of the Shield of the Americas , which some have dubbed the new Plan Condor. Senator Ana Crispín accused him of handing lawmakers QR codes that she alleged were tied to payments for their votes. Kathryn Ledebur, director of the Andean Information Network in Cochabamba, speculated “that the Paz government will hand Mariaca over to the DEA [very quickly], just like they did with Marset, no extradition process or anything,” referring to Uruguayan kingpin Sebastián Marset, captured in a DEA-backed operation in Bolivia in March and sent to the United States. “Apparently, getting your visa revoked doesn’t mean you won’t get to know the US — quite the opposite.” She may be right. The day after the sanctions list was released, Defense Minister Ernesto Justiniano said the case could lead to “a judicial step in the United States, probably an extradition request.” Vice President Lara Says He’s the Next Target In the following days, sitting Vice President Edmand Lara, a former police captain who was pushed out of the Bolivian National Police after publicly denouncing corruption inside it, sounded the alarm that he could be next. Speaking from Madrid, Lara said he received warnings “from within the executive” that police were preparing to plant evidence in order to arrest him, and he named a police colonel, Marcelo Ferrufino, as the man behind it. “I fear for my physical integrity and for my life,” Lara said. “This would be a frame-up for political ends, to silence me.” The government has not responded publicly. Lara was elected on Paz’s ticket, likely winning him the election, but he broke with the president in December 2025, declaring himself in “constructive opposition” as the president abandoned his moderate positions to align himself with the far-right Santa Cruz business interests that he had defeated electorally. Lara has since become one of the most vocal critics of Paz and his security cabinet. He backed the union-led protests in May, pressed for transparency over Cerimedo’s role in the government, released audio recordings implicating the adviser, and has demanded that Washington’s hand be pulled back from Bolivia’s security and politics. After Mariaca’s arrest, the vice president warned that “no foreign police agent, whether from the DEA or any other institution, can exercise arrest powers in our territory outside Bolivian law,” refusing to treat a US sanctions list as grounds for prosecuting Bolivian officials. Rule by Emergency Since June 20, the Paz administration has governed under a “ state of exception ,” curtailing civil and political rights, including the right to protest. Road blockades are banned, mass gatherings are restricted, and the military is deployed alongside the police. The emergency powers were declared after fifty days of protests and blockades by Bolivian unions, campesino and indigenous organizations, and the opposition. The protests were triggered by Law 1720, which allowed small agricultural holdings, legally protected from seizure, to be converted into medium-size properties that could be mortgaged to banks. Indigenous and campesino groups saw it as a first step toward handing their lands, redistributed after the 1952 Revolution, to “more productive” sectors; opposition politicians said it was written on behalf of the large and politically dominant agribusiness sector concentrated in Santa Cruz, the country’s conservative economic capital. After protesters marched more than a thousand kilometers from Pando to La Paz, President Paz repealed the law on May 14. But by then, the movement had widened into a revolt against the end of fuel subsidies, the imported “junk gasoline” that was wrecking engines, and the worst economic crisis in decades. As the government moved toward emergency rule, Claudia Herbas, a deputy for the Alianza Popular opposition who introduced the bill to repeal the decree, warned that coercive measures would only escalate the violence, urging a return to the negotiating table. Instead, the blockades were broken by force. Bolivia’s Ombudsman’s Office recorded twenty-two deaths over the course of the conflict, along with eighty-eight injured and 583 arrested. The Inter-American Commission on Human Rights found that police used excessive force, in some cases in coordination with far-right vigilante groups . The protests were broken within days, but the state of exception continues. On September 17, the Assembly extended it through mid-December, with Paz arguing it would let the government act against “narcoterrorism.” The Mariaca affair fits neatly into that project. It hands an embattled president, whose approval rating had collapsed to 21 percent by September, a fresh justification for emergency rule long after the blockades have ended. And it lets him centralize power and delegitimize a judiciary that has occasionally checked him, even after he had already abolished the Ministry of Justice and turned the machinery of the state against his political enemies. This is the first time a state of exception has been invoked under Bolivia’s 2009 constitution; the last comparable measure was the 2008 state of siege in Pando , declared after the Porvenir massacre of campesinos. These emergency powers echo darker chapters of Bolivian history, both of them provoked by Washington. In 1971, Hugo Banzer seized power in a US-supported coup and ruled by decree until 1978, banning unions, jailing and disappearing opponents, and joining Plan Condor; when he returned as an elected president, he declared a state of siege during the 2000 Cochabamba Water War. And in 2019, after the coup d’état that forced Morales from office, the interim government of Jeanine Áñez issued a decree shielding the armed forces from prosecution; within days, security forces killed at least twenty people in the Sacaba and Senkata massacres. The Trump White House hailed the coup against Morales as “a significant moment for democracy in the Western Hemisphere.” MAGA’s Man in La Paz Mariaca was elected by the Assembly in October 2024, during the government of former socialist President Luis Arce, to a six-year term. Arce himself has been jailed in preventive detention since December by the pro-US Paz administration; just last week, a judge refused to release him despite illness. The other socialist former president, Evo Morales, has been holed up in his compound in the Chapare coca-growing region, where he is shielded by supporters from an arrest warrant. Paz has threatened that Morales’s “days are numbered .” Morales has interpreted Mariaca’s arrest as evidence of who is really running the country. “It confirms that in Bolivia, the United States governs,” he said . “It is open and direct interference.” The point of the operation, he added, was to decide “whom they will persecute and detain in order to save Cerimedo — and saving Cerimedo is saving Rodrigo Paz and his family.” The investigation Mariaca was leading goes to the heart of the Paz government. “ MAGA’s man in Latin America” kept an office on the twenty-third floor of the presidential palace, sat in on cabinet meetings, and controlled the president’s communications; one Bolivian analyst called him “the closest thing to a prime minister the country had.” Cerimedo also worked for Milei and Kast, and de la Espriella’s campaign has ties to his former business partner. Milei, Kast, and de la Espriella are all now presidents of their respective countries. At a ceremony at Mar-a-Lago in February, where Cerimedo was honored as the year’s top Hispanic political consultant, he thanked his business partner Brad Parscale, Donald Trump’s former campaign manager, who has since registered as a foreign agent for Israel . Photos have also surfaced of him with Donald Trump Jr . Since his arrest, the powerful in Bolivia have kept their distance; Paz insists that “Mr Cerimedo never had the authorization to represent [him].” But Cerimedo first cut his teeth in Brazil. Between the two rounds of the 2022 presidential election, Eduardo Bolsonaro, son of then President Jair Bolsonaro, traveled to Buenos Aires to meet Cerimedo . Days after Lula’s victory, Cerimedo hosted a live stream on his outlet, La Derecha Diario, claiming that voting machines built before 2020 had skewed the count toward Lula. Close to 400,000 people watched the stresm before Brazil’s electoral court ordered it taken down, and Bolsonaro’s Liberal Party leaned on the same claims in its bid to annul the votes cast on those machines. In 2024, Brazil’s Federal Police named Cerimedo as one of the “nuclei” of the coup plot that culminated in the riots in Brasília of January 8, 2023. He was the only foreigner to be charged in the plot. In late July, less than a month before his arrest in Bolivia, Cerimedo joined Eduardo Bolsonaro for an hour-long live stream, reviving the debunked vote-tampering claims just two days after Flávio Bolsonaro, whose presidential bid performed above expectations in Sunday’s first round , repeated the falsehood about the voting machines to foreign diplomats. The Cover-Up Cerimedo’s partner, Nadia Beller, survived the attempt on her life in which she was shot three times, though her pregnancy did not. Beller immediately accused Cerimedo of ordering the hit. He was arrested hours later at Viru Viru airport and has since been placed in preventive detention, first for attempted femicide and then also for illicit enrichment . In an interview with Jacobin , Beller indicated that “police raided the prosecutor’s office without a court order” and warned that “they are going to make the evidence against Cerimedo disappear.” The arrest, she told me, is “clearly linked to Washington, illegal, and [is being] used to go after the opposition.” Prosecutors were examining Cerimedo’s alleged links to drug-trafficking networks, including audio recordings released by Vice President Lara in which a voice attributed to Cerimedo discusses payments of $15,000 per small plane and coordination with Franz Cabrera, then head of the national antinarcotics police. Cerimedo denies the allegations. The case was being pursued by the Public Ministry that Mariaca led until he was jailed without due process. The day after the arrest, the La Paz departmental prosecutor handling the Cerimedo file, Luis Carlos Tórrez, resigned . In a public letter after the Assembly installed Urioste, Beller listed twenty-six corruption cases that have surfaced in less than a year of Paz’s government and asked whether the new attorney general would investigate any of them. Beller also pointed to Washington’s record. Former Honduran President Juan Orlando Hernández was sentenced in the United States to forty-five years for conspiring to import cocaine and turning Honduras into a narco-state, and Trump pardoned him. “It makes us think that justice never reaches Trump’s friends; they are forgiven everything,” she wrote. “And since Rodrigo Paz and Cerimedo are now anointed with his grace, they will go unpunished.” She recalled, too, that Minister Oviedo had warned Bolivians that “either you are with us or you face the consequences” and that “those on the other side will be fought,” and compared his statements to those of Luis Arce Gómez, interior minister of the 1980 García Meza dictatorship, who warned that opponents “have to walk around with their will under their arm.” Luis Alberto Echazú, a former mining minister under Morales, went further: “The rulers who, like Rodrigo Paz, have handed over state political decisions to these kinds of foreign agents disguised as advisers must be put on trial for treason against the homeland,” he said. One former adviser to Paz, who resigned his government post over policy disagreements, alleged that there is an effort inside the government to cover up Cerimedo’s role. “It is clear that nobody involved is being honest about what transpired,” said the adviser, who requested anonymity to avoid retaliation. A New Plan Condor Bolivia has become one of the focal points of Washington’s new war on drugs, now under the name of “narcoterrorism,” a label that the administration has used to mobilize the resources and legal authorities of the post-9/11 war on terror. Bolivia, coincidentally, sits on an estimated twenty-three million metric tons of lithium, among the largest reserves on earth. The Arce administration’s extraction deals with Chinese and Russian firms have been frozen since Paz took office and turned toward the United States. A friendly government in La Paz is a foothold in the heart of the continent and a rebuke to Beijing’s growing influence in the region. As it was under the Nixon and Reagan administrations, the drug war has also proven a convenient excuse to go after political opponents. When the blockades in Bolivia peaked in June, Deputy Secretary of State Christopher Landau called the protests “a coup financed by this perverse alliance between politics and organized crime”; Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth warned that “Bolivia must not allow itself to fall prey to the old status quo of narco-terrorist dominance”; and Marco Rubio vowed that Washington “will not allow criminals and drug traffickers to overthrow democratically elected leaders.” Paz himself branded the protesters “narco-terrorists,” and a number of officials in the Trump administration’s orbit have also painted Evo Morales as a terrorist. “During this state of exception, Paz has gone after unions, opposition politicians, journalists, activists, indigenous groups, and anyone who stands in his way politically,” one activist who has helped lead protests in El Alto told me. “This is clearly part of a bigger plan to go after the Left.” The United States has targeted other elected officials and members of the judiciary in the region, including Colombian Senator Martha Isabel Peralta , an indigenous leftist from the Historic Pact, and the Peruvian judge Juan Carlos Núñez, who ruled against regulators at the Chinese-built port of Chancay. Former Colombian President Gustavo Petro has described the Shield of the Americas as a smokescreen for bringing Washington’s adversaries to trial while protecting its allies, a twenty-first-century Plan Condor and a “political apartheid against anyone who thinks differently from the owners of the White House.” Under Plan Condor, the United States helped install, arm, and protect a string of brutal right-wing military dictatorships across South America, most notoriously Augusto Pinochet’s in Chile, as they coordinated the kidnapping, torture, and murder of leftists across borders. Another US protégé was Peru’s Alberto Fujimori, whose spy chief, Vladimiro Montesinos, was on the CIA’s payroll,. and who was convicted in 2009 for death-squad massacres that Peru’s Supreme Court deemed crimes against humanity. His daughter, Keiko Fujimori, took office in July as president of Peru. As it happens, her adviser, Carlos Díaz-Rosillo, was photographed with Cerimedo in Peru over a year ago, before the official launch of her campaign. Open for US Business President Paz has also been working hard to court US investment, which he says was driven away by “socialism” and “constant political instability,” including the protests, which he blamed for Coca-Cola’s decision to scrap a planned $380 million investment, much of it slated for El Alto. In September, the Assembly approved a $1.9 billion loan program from the International Monetary Fund (IMF) to back Paz’s economic restructuring; the IMF board signed off on October 2, releasing a first $214 million the same week Mariaca was jailed. The political pivot was even reflected in La Paz’s famous state-owned cable cars: this summer, thirteen cabins were wrapped in images of American flags and the Statue of Liberty in ad space sold to the US embassy for its “Freedom 250” celebration of American independence. Bolivia joined the Shield of the Americas at its founding in March. In May, the DEA returned to Bolivia for the first time since Morales expelled it in 2008, along with the US ambassador, for political interference. The two countries have resumed military cooperation after a twenty-year rupture. DEA intelligence underpinned the operation against Mariaca, and Marset was handed to the United States after a DEA-backed capture. After the arrests, Secretary of State Marco Rubio tied the operation directly to the anti-drug-trafficking commitments Bolivia made at the Shield of the Americas leaders’ summit the week before, and fifteen member governments of the alliance issued a joint statement backing the Bolivian government’s actions. The war on drugs is once again being used as a pretext to prosecute political adversaries across the region. These brazen moves will keep ramping up as right-wing power backed by the Trump administration consolidates itself. articles.title: Coal Revival
articles.author: Marcus Baram
articles.content: The opinions expressed here are solely the author's and do not reflect the opinions or beliefs of the LA Progressive. Craig Unit 1, a coal-fired power plant distinguished by tall exhaust smokestacks that rise above a rolling landscape in northwestern Colorado, was scheduled to close for good at the end of 2025 amid pressure from environmental advocates, public interest groups and state officials. But on Dec. 30, Energy Secretary Chris Wright ordered it to keep burning coal. The unit had suffered a mechanical failure 11 days earlier and was not even running. Wright has since renewed the order three times — most recently on Sept. 25, extending the plant’s life through Christmas Day, a full year past its retirement date. Its operator, Tri-State Generation and Transmission, is a nonprofit rural cooperative, and in January it joined co-owner Platte River Power Authority, a public power agency, in arguing that Wright’s orders violate the Constitution and federal law — a fight that has since reached a federal appeals court in Washington, D.C. A co-op and a municipal utility suing the executive branch for the right to close their own coal plant was not what Congress had in mind in 1935, when it wrote the emergency provision that the Energy Department is now leaning on. Data centers and gas pump prices have dominated the energy story in this midterm cycle — polls show broad opposition to the artificial intelligence build-out over utility bills and grid strain. But with five weeks until Election Day, a second tier of climate and energy battles is running through campaigns in Michigan, Colorado, Indiana and beyond: forced coal plant extensions, canceled plans for offshore wind farms, repealed clean energy tax credits, drought, state preemption of local climate rules and a drumbeat of federal rollbacks. None of these issues poll as high as affordability. But all of them, say the people trying to turn them into votes, are essential to the affordability debate. The Plant Nobody Asked to Keep Starting in May 2025, the Energy Department invoked Section 202(c) of the Federal Power Act to order Consumers Energy’s J.H. Campbell plant in West Olive, Michigan, to stay online past its planned retirement, then renewed the order five more times. Similar mandates followed for Craig and for the Schahfer and Culley plants in Indiana, each justified by grid reliability. On Sept. 11, a unanimous D.C. Circuit panel, in an opinion written by Judge Cornelia Pillard, ruled that the first two Campbell orders were illegal — no genuine emergency existed to justify overriding Michigan’s regulators. Ari Peskoe, director of the Electricity Law Initiative at Harvard Law School, said the provision had been dormant for decades after some early wartime use. “Over the past 20 to 30 years it’s really been used almost exclusively for weather-related events,” he said, “and it only lasts a few days.” Nothing like Wright’s coal orders had been tried. “In every prior instance there’s been some entity, whether a utility, a grid operator or a state regulator, that’s asked for these orders. Here it’s [the Department of Energy] acting on its own,” he said. “No one had asked for it. And to the contrary, some had said, ’Please don’t do this.’” The administration has until roughly the end of October to decide whether to appeal. If it lets the ruling stand, Peskoe said, “I think the other orders for the other plants will fall pretty quickly.” Related: GOP Candidate Exploits Data Center Backlash to Hit Solar, Wind in Wisconsin Who Pays Utility giant Consumers Energy put the net cost of running Campbell from May 23, 2025, through June 30 of this year at $295 million, after wholesale market revenue. Michigan Attorney General Dana Nessel’s office has cited that figure, against nearly $600 million in savings the retirement was supposed to deliver. In August, federal regulators let Consumers Energy spread the costs across the grid’s north and central regions — from North Dakota to Indiana. That means Wisconsin ratepayers, whose share one estimate puts at $117 million, could wind up paying for a Michigan coal plant. The recent appeals court decision overturning the Energy Department’s order could spare taxpayers those costs . Brian Wheeler, spokesperson for Consumers Energy, said the utility would work to ensure “everyone who benefits from power from the Campbell plant across the Midwest pays their fair share.” Nessel , who has challenged all six orders, said, “This administration does not get to invent fake emergencies to bypass the rule of law.” Three States, Three Fights The coal plants have become a factor in the midterm elections for a key seat in Michigan. The Campbell plant sits in the 4th Congressional District, where Rep. Bill Huizenga, a Republican, is defending a traditionally red seat against Democratic state Sen. Sean McCann of Kalamazoo. Huizenga cheered the first order; constituents answered with marches on his office under signs reading, “My asthma and my wallet can’t afford coal.” “If you’re seeing your electric bills go up, that has happened because of this,” McCann told a crowd in Saugatuck in August. “This should be shut down.” Related: Arizona’s Rising Electric Bills Are Reshaping the 2026 Midterms Huizenga blamed Gov. Gretchen Whitmer “and her Green New Deal cronies in the state Legislature like Sean McCann,” arguing that “forcing the premature closure of cheap, reliable power plants is punishing hardworking Michiganders who just want to keep their lights on without going broke.” The fight runs up the ballot. Nessel, who recently joined McCann at a roundtable on the Campbell plant, is term limited, and the race to succeed her as attorney general has become a referendum on whether Michigan should keep suing. Democrat Eli Savit, the Washtenaw County prosecutor, pledged to continue the Campbell litigation, while Republican Doug Lloyd, the Eaton County prosecutor, has declined to take a position on the plant and accused Nessel of politicizing the office. Climate Power senior adviser Jesse Lee said the issue had ripened with time and is starting to galvanize voters. “The longer these decisions have sat out in the sun, the worse they stank,” he said. “It might have a ring of common sense — oh, we need more energy — but people caught on to that: ’Wait, this is actually costing me more money. There’s one guy who supports it and one guy who’s against it.’” A poll commissioned by the Environmental Defense Fund in West Michigan found 71% of respondents said their utility bills had risen too much, and 51% favored closing the Campbell plant, as opposed to 32% who want it kept open. But the coal industry insists otherwise, with a September National Mining Association poll in which 58% of Americans supported government efforts to keep coal plants open. Colorado’s version runs through the 3rd Congressional District, where Rep. Jeff Hurd, a Republican and former co-op lawyer, asked the Energy Department to intervene and keep Xcel’s Comanche plant in Pueblo running. Hurd praised the Craig order as a correction to a state energy policy “driven by ideology instead of reality.” His Democratic challenger, Dwayne Romero of Aspen, is running on affordability, accusing Hurd of “rubberstamping reckless policies that raise our costs.” Statewide, Sen. Michael Bennet called the Energy Department order part of a federal “revenge tour” against Colorado, and Attorney General Phil Weiser, the Democratic nominee for governor, has challenged every coal-fired plant renewal, warning it “will result in unnecessary costs passed onto Coloradans in higher electric bills and more pollution in the region.” But in Craig, a small coal town near the Wyoming border, Mayor Chris Nichols welcomed the short-term jobs resulting from the order. The cost so far is unknown: Tri-State spokesman Mark Stutz said generator-specific data is confidential. Indiana is the outlier — the orders have a cheerleader in the governor’s office and no competitive race to carry them, since both plants sit in safe Republican House seats. Gov. Mike Braun praised the latest renewal , saying it would “help protect Hoosiers from higher energy costs and keep the power on.” Related: Military Family Food Insecurity Surges as Grocery Costs and Support Gaps Deepen But the utilities disagree, with CenterPoint asking the Energy Department in February to let the Culley order lapse, calling the power plant “inefficient and increasingly unreliable.” NIPSCO, one of Indiana’s largest power companies, said both Schahfer units covered by the orders remained offline for maintenance, and asked federal regulators in August to approve about $38 million in cost recovery for the first quarter — a bill for a plant that was not running. On top of that, the utility has outraged customers, who experienced a more than 25% jump in their bills last year. The pushback has come from statehouse Democrats like Rep. Carey Hamilton, who said Hoosiers were “being asked to foot the bill for a decision they had no say in.” Galvanizing, or Not As to other climate and energy issues, their impact on the elections depend on whether a voter can feel the issue, such as dwindling water supplies. Federal cuts to Arizona’s Colorado River supply in August pushed water to the top of the state’s campaign messaging — Gov. Katie Hobbs is running an ad declaring, “Arizona’s water is for Arizonans,” while Republicans accuse her of failing to negotiate a fair water rights deal. Along with Colorado farmers getting no water after a dismal snowpack and Corpus Christi potentially owing Texas $235 million for a desalination plant that was never built, the crisis highlights how climate change is being experienced by many Americans through higher water bills, exacerbating the affordability challenge. The electric vehicle tax credit repeal has galvanized donors more than voters. The One Big Beautiful Bill’s elimination of the credit cast a pall over 2026 sales, and its wind and solar phaseout spawned a super PAC, the Invest in Tomorrow Coalition, that bills its work as a “Revenge Tour” and has already claimed five Republican primary scalps — including Rep. Chip Roy, who lost a runoff election in May for Texas attorney general. Four House Republicans, among them Rep. Mike Lawler of New York, have introduced a bill to restore the EV credits and House Democrats have made reinstating such credits a major part of their governing agenda. Offshore wind is a courtroom story more than a voting booth one. Nine states have sued over federal deals paying developers more than $1.5 billion to abandon leases on the condition they reinvest in oil, gas or geothermal instead. The League of Conservation Voters’ David Shadburn put the estimated taxpayer tab for blocking cheaper power at nearly $4 billion. Florida’s HB 1217 , which stripped cities of climate authority and outraged Democratic mayors, has been duplicated across the country but seems to have little visible traction with voters. And on Sept. 14 the EPA finalized its repeal of most Biden-era power plant rules, while the House passed the Ratepayer Protection Act, which the League of Conservation Voters dismissed as window dressing. Neither one seems to have galvanized voters, though some Democratic candidates have mentioned them in their campaigns. Whether voters can parse any of it is another matter. Related: The Marines Cut Family Support Staff: Then the Iran War Started “To some extent it’s all a bit of a blur for voters,” said Lee, the Climate Power adviser. “But it’s all kind of accumulated into one cloud of corruption. They just understand that they’re paying more every which way they look.” As for what lands last, he pointed north. It is getting chilly, and people are starting to read about what it will cost to heat their homes — a problem for Lawler in New York and Sen. Susan Collins in Maine, and for anyone else on the ballot above the Mason-Dixon line. “That’s the kind of story voters are going to be reading about right before they head into the voting booth,” noted Lee. Capital & Main

articles.title: China Is Winning
articles.author: Tom Engelhardt
articles.content: The opinions expressed here are solely the author's and do not reflect the opinions or beliefs of the LA Progressive. I wonder if our ever stranger, more Trumpian country would look any better were I to trade in the kind of glasses I’ve worn since I was a nearsighted kid in fourth grade for what have become known as Meta’s “ Pervert glasses ,” complete with camera and audio. In some way, though, this old guy may just want to turn in any kind of glasses whatsoever. Not only do I feel a lack of desire to record our new (but also unbearably old) world, moment by moment, day by day, week by week, but this is increasingly a world I might prefer not even to see. After all, it does seem as if, in some strange but essential way, we humans—if, of course, Donald Trump even is a human being and not a Martian masquerading (not particularly effectively) as one of us—may be all too prepared to end this world of ours, at least as we’ve known it. Of course, such an ending would be exactly what we’ve feared for so long: that humanity was the ultimate in destruction. The only genuinely unexpected thing about such a reality, I suspect, is that it might not happen as we once imagined (via nuclear weapons) in a distinctly short space of time, but in a slow-motion version of the apocalypse that fits all too well with the slow-motion arrival of what we’ve come to know as climate change. Keep in mind that, in these years, Americans elected a president (twice, with a brief, aged intermission) who has given the very idea of end times new meaning. It’s also true that we’re in a world where (leaving aside Vladimir Putin’s flailing war in Ukraine and Donald Trump’s pathetic all-American war in Iran) the latest version of a great imperial power no longer seems intent on seizing foreign territory the way such powers have done throughout our history. Buy the Book Amid this chaotic world of ours, in fact, give China full credit. No, not for its political system, of course, but for the fact that, unlike any other great power in human memory, aside from its month-long war with Vietnam in 1979 and its border skirmishes with India as this decade began, it’s extended its power and influence globally without trying to seize a single country or going to war in any way whatsoever. The only thing it’s seized, in fact, is significant control over the future production of green power , which, given our planet and where it’s headed right now, simply couldn’t have been a smarter “imperial” way to go. And as an imperial approach to global power, it also couldn’t be both more historically out of the ordinary and, on this strangely embattled planet of ours, more intelligent. After all, we humans are already functionally at war, day and night, week after week, month after month, year after year, with our world as a livable place for us, not to speak of everything else from mountain lions and elephants to eels and cockroaches. Honestly, it’s more stunning than you ever see described in our mainstream media. I’m thinking, of course, of how we’re literally heating this planet toward the boiling point. This summer, after all, was the hottest in both Europe and the United States in all of recorded history. Imagine that! And imagine this as well: in such a context, in 2024, the citizens of the still most powerful country on the planet reelected a man who can’t even imagine that the world is getting hotter (and hotter and hotter) by the year. Think of him, given what he’s had to say about climate change, as the “ con job “ president or perhaps even President Heat. In his bizarre ignorance of the subject, think of him, in fact, as quite literally turning this planet’s future over to Earth’s rising power, China, and believe me, that’s no small thing to do. No wonder the normally unsmiling Chinese leader Xi Jinping had such a grin on his face during his recent meeting with President Trump at the White House. He knows that, while his country is investing ever more in producing (and selling) a greener planet, the American president—from Venezuela ( “ the biggest oil deal in world history ”) to Iran —should be considered the fossil-fuel king par excellence and so, not our future, but our past writ all too large. Related: Donald Trump and a World at the Boiling Point A New Definition of Imperial Decline So here we are in—well, what century could it be when two of the greatest powers on Earth are still fighting wars with two lesser countries (Ukraine and Iran), while the third is intent on turning both Donald Trump’s America and Vladimir Putin’s Russia into ancient history? Those two old-fashioned imperial powers are now flailing, if not simply failing, while the rising imperial power, China, seems all too ready to conquer in a distinctly imperial fashion. In the case of China, however, we’re not talking about territory, but a very different kind of conquest on this planet. After all, with its proliferating green energy industries, its near monopoly of the new field of electric vehicles, and its sale of green everything to the rest of the planet, China is giving the very word “imperial” a radically new meaning, even as it, too, rises (financially and otherwise) on—quite honestly—the backs of a future humanity, including its own people, and does so on an unnervingly different planet. And of all people, I really shouldn’t be shocked by any of this since, in my early teens, I was already drawing a fantasy map of the Chinese conquest of the world (which, believe it or not, I still possess). And keep in mind that, after all these centuries, thanks to the way we humans are heating up this globe of ours, we’re already in a very different kind of imperial world, even if “our” president hasn’t the slightest idea that that’s so. Honestly, at this very moment in history, there simply couldn’t be a better definition of imperial decline than Donald J. Trump as president (twice!) of the United States. If anything, he’s giving the very concept of decline new meaning. Related: The Planet Is Burning—and We’re Still Making War Imagine this, after all: an American president on a planet growing ever hotter whose key goal is to foster the energy that’s already broiling this world of—well, honestly, I don’t really think you can say “ours” anymore, can you? Though our mainstream media (which generally underplays the significance of climate change) never suggests it, Donald J. Trump should be considered the definition of a globally suicidal president. And if there are history books in our future to record it, even a theoretically rising imperial power like China is undoubtedly going to find itself in an historically different situation on a planet that’s going down, down, down (at least when it comes to human comfort and habitability). Honestly, I suspect that these days we’re all wearing “Pervert glasses,” with our vision of this world twisted increasingly upside down. Honestly (to be repetitive), I’m already sweating! Tom's Substack

articles.title: Marx Believed Meaningful Work Was Central to the Good Life
articles.author: Jan Kandiyali
articles.content: Not too long ago, a wave of books written by left-wing and liberal commentators appeared celebrating a future in which work would be a thing of the past. The increased productivity of technology would free humans from drudgery and allow them to focus on cultural pursuits and spend more time making friends or finding love, these polemics alleged. Amid the near-daily stream of stories warning about the disastrous social effects that artificial intelligence may have, not just on the labor market but on people’s literacy and numeracy, this earlier mood seems at best misguided. In his recently published book , Flourishing Together: Karl Marx’s Vision of the Good Society , Jan Kandiyali, a professor of philosophy at Durham University in England, argues that his subject’s views about work and the good life have been deeply misunderstood. Yes, Marx was a profound critic of capitalism. He saw the system as exploitative and harmful to human relations of friendship and love. But he also thought that contributing productively to society was a vital component of the good life. In a wide-ranging discussion, Kandiyali tells Jacobin why socialists mustn’t abandon this vision. The path to building a better society runs through, rather than past, recognizing the social value of work. Hugo de Camps We usually think of Marx mainly as a critic of capitalism. In Flourishing Together , you argue that his work also contains a positive account of human flourishing. What is, in your view, a good society for Marx? Jan Kandiyali I agree that people generally think of Marx as a critic of capitalism. The book is motivated by two thoughts: First, that Marx was more concerned with the question of what a good society would look like than people tend to think. And second, that it is a mistake for socialists to confine themselves to criticism of existing society without offering an account of an alternative. As G. A. Cohen once said, unless you write recipes for the cookshops of the future, there is no guarantee you will get the food you like. I understand a good society as one that enables its members to flourish. The word “enables” is important here. It is not about guaranteeing that people flourish or forcing them to, but about giving them the real opportunity to do so. Moreover, in Marx’s view, a vital component of human flourishing is self-realization in work. So, a good society is one that enables self-realization in work, among other things. Hugo de Camps How, exactly, do you understand work in this context? Jan Kandiyali Defining work is difficult, and I do not offer a strict definition. I am interested in self-realization in work, understood as activity that enables people to develop their powers and capacities while also meeting the needs of others. That differs from employment understood simply as wage labor. In my sense of the term, people can work without being employed, for example through charity work. Conversely, someone can be employed without working in this sense. Think of David Graeber’s “bullshit jobs” or work that is actively harmful, such as maximizing the addictiveness of gambling technologies. You can receive a wage without engaging in the kind of self-realizing work that I am interested in. Hugo de Camps At the center of the book is what you call the mutualist interpretation, contrasted with the parallelist view associated with G. A. Cohen and Jon Elster. On the parallelist view, individuals may flourish alongside one another, but not necessarily through one another. What would you say is missing from this reading, and why do you find the mutualist interpretation more convincing? Jan Kandiyali The parallelist reading, which is my term, says that people realize themselves simply by developing their powers and capacities. They may do so in ways that benefit others, but this is not required: their activity might simply benefit themselves. Cohen illustrates this with the example of a jazz band. Cohen says: one way of understanding Marx’s vision of the good society is to imagine a jazz band in which each player is motivated by their own self-realization. Now, in this jazz band, each player needs their fellow musicians to provide the music for their self-realization. But they do not value their cooperation or the fact that they are providing the conditions for one another’s self-realization. On the parallelist view, then, we achieve self-realization alongside others, through our parallel projects of self-realization, but not necessarily through contributing to one another’s flourishing. I contrast it with the mutualist interpretation. On the mutualist interpretation, people realize themselves through providing others with the various goods and services they need to pursue their flourishing. So, the mutualist interpretation is a more social and relational vision of the good society. Now, to turn directly to your question, the short answer is that the parallelist vision leaves out the value of solidarity. By solidarity, I mean concern for others and finding value in activities through which we contribute to their lives. I think Marx and the socialist tradition more generally saw these solidaristic relationships as part of human flourishing. Without them, your life may go well in some respects, but you are missing something important. In a nutshell, that is what the parallelist account leaves out. Hugo de Camps You describe mutual self-realization as developing our capacities in ways that provide others with the goods and services they need to flourish. Voluntary care seems a clear case, but what about entertainment or luxury goods? Put differently: Does mutual flourishing depend on distinguishing genuine human needs from preferences shaped by the market? Jan Kandiyali I understand needs as things required for people to flourish. That means that we can distinguish genuine needs from preferences shaped by the market — what Marxists, particularly in the tradition of the Frankfurt School, have called false needs. We might desire certain things we do not need. But at the same time, we should not think of needs in too restricted a way. Marx had a broad and rich understanding of what we need to flourish. In his early writings, he contrasts the wealth and poverty of capitalism with the “rich human being” and “rich human need” associated with communism. The ideal is not merely to satisfy basic physical needs. Cultural goods, aesthetic enjoyment, and entertainment, for example, also count as needs. Marx’s ideal was not one of an austere life of self-denial, nor should ours be. Hugo de Camps Recognition by others forms part of your account of socialization through productive activity, but recognition can also be gained through friendship, care, political activity, or artistic creation. Is there anything distinctive, in your view, about work as a source of self-realization? Jan Kandiyali I am not claiming that the recognition we receive through friendship, family, or other activities is unimportant. But there is, I think, something distinctive about the recognition we receive for our productive contributions. Recognition within the family or among friends typically has a certain character. Especially within the family, it tends to be relatively unconditional: it does not typically depend upon your specific achievements. In productive activity, by contrast, you are recognized primarily for what you contribute. If I write a book, for example, other people assess its merits and shortcomings and recognize me on the basis of that contribution. So, my answer to your question would be quite Hegelian: we have needs for different types of recognition — as family members, friends, producers, and citizens. These forms are distinct and cannot simply substitute for one another. Hugo de Camps You present Marx’s vision of socialism as an alternative to liberal egalitarian theories of justice such as John Rawls’s. While liberal egalitarians focus primarily on distribution, your reading of Marx emphasizes production, self-realization, and social relations. What can this account explain that a theory centered on distribution cannot? Jan Kandiyali The liberal egalitarianism of Rawls and his immediate followers is an impressive body of work, but I think it has two limitations. First, its focus on distribution leaves out the sphere of production. Perhaps surprisingly, one of the first people to make this point was the libertarian philosopher Robert Nozick, who argued that liberal egalitarians such as Rawls can write as though resources exist in a “big social pot” waiting to be distributed. But obviously enough, those goods have to be produced in the first place. So, liberal egalitarianism has traditionally lacked a theory of what Lucas Stanczyk calls “productive justice.” This lacuna has, to a large degree, been addressed in recent years. (For a Marxist theory of it, I recommend Paul Gomberg’s excellent book , How to Make Opportunity Equal: Race and Contributive Justice .) Second, the focus on justice leaves out a concern with the good society and what it means for people’s lives to go well. Justice is sometimes glossed as giving people their due. But people can receive their due while living bad lives. For example, they might get their due but pursue worthless conceptions of the good, such as amassing an endless supply of consumer goods. Or they might be treated fairly by social institutions but lack any solidarity with their fellows. Concerns with justice and distribution are obviously important, but they leave out important dimensions of human flourishing. So Marx gives us a way of bringing a concern with work and human flourishing back into debates in political philosophy. Hugo de Camps In the book, you present a critique of post-work politics and argue that socialism should aim to transform work rather than reduce its role. Can you explain why? Jan Kandiyali There is a divide between socialists who seek to transform work and those who seek to reduce its importance. My book belongs squarely in the former camp, as I think that work can be an important good for us when it is organized in the right way. I believe that a life in which everything we needed appeared like manna from heaven would be far from ideal. In such a world, human beings would no longer need one another to provide the goods and services required for flourishing. We could, of course, still read poetry, play football, or watch films together, but the collective activity of meeting one another’s needs would disappear. This implies that a post-work world would be, in one respect, worse than one in which our labor is required. Current anxieties about AI and technologically driven unemployment seem to me to support this view. Part of the worry about AI is that people will lose an income, but I do not think this is their sole concern. People are also worried about what they would do if AI took their jobs. Of course, many people also want to work less and have more time for family, friends, and other activities, but I do not think that most people want to eliminate work altogether. Hugo de Camps If productive contribution is an important part of human flourishing, does this risk creating new hierarchies between forms of work? And how does your account accommodate those who, because of disability or illness, may be unable to participate in productive activity? Jan Kandiyali I will take up the issue of hierarchy and the issue of disability and illness separately. With regard to hierarchy between different forms of work, the book offers a simple solution. A standard Marxist line is that automation will solve the problem of drudgery. I am not against automating drudgery, but I am skeptical that it can completely solve the issue here. My view is that the drudgery should be shared among everyone able to perform it. That would help overcome hierarchies between different forms of work because drudgery would then be done by everyone. With regard to those who cannot work because of illness and disability, we should be cautious of thinking that the ill or the disabled cannot work. As proponents of the social model of disability have argued, much depends on the social environment. Maybe some people cannot work now. But with appropriate adjustments, they might be able to. Of course, it is true that even with all the adjustments, some people still will not be able to work. In Marx’s vision of the good society, the relevant principle is “From each according to their abilities, to each according to their needs!” This means that those who cannot work will not be materially any worse off than those who can, since needs are met irrespective of prior labor contribution. However, it is an implication of the view — and perhaps a difficult one — that people who are unable to produce miss out on a vital component of human flourishing. Hugo de Camps How do you see the relationship between ideal theory and more immediate political questions? Jan Kandiyali Flourishing Together is primarily a work of ideal, or utopian, political theory. It asks what a genuinely good society might look like and uses that ideal to critique capitalism. The final chapter does discuss issues of transition, but it discusses transition from what Marx called the lower phase of communism to the higher. It does not provide a detailed route from present-day capitalism. Clarifying the level at which the argument operates is important when we turn to more immediate political questions. My criticism of universal basic income (UBI), for example, does not mean that UBI could not be useful now, perhaps as a way of reducing poverty. Questions like that depend on various concerns about institutions, public support, trade unions, and political organization. I do not deal directly with these issues in the book, but I think it is a very good thing that more work within political philosophy is now considering these questions. Overall, I see nonideal political philosophy and the ideal project of imagining a good society as complementary.
